journal_name: IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering

abstracts.abstract: The fundamental assumptions underlying existing heterogeneous graph neural networks suffer from semantic ambiguity when processing multi-relational knowledge structures. This paper proposes a knowledge-aware aggregation paradigm that fundamentally reconceptualizes information propagation in heterogeneous networks. Unlike conventional message-passing mechanisms that treat node features and relation types independently, our framework introduces semantic correlation functions that capture the intrinsic interdependence between structural patterns and knowledge semantics. We develop a novel theoretical framework based on spectral graph theory to analyze the expressiveness boundaries of heterogeneous representation learning, proving that our approach can approximate arbitrary set functions on heterogeneous subgraphs. Furthermore, we establish rigorous generalization bounds that reveal how knowledge semantics transfer across relation types. Experimental results on three benchmark knowledge graphs demonstrate that the proposed paradigm achieves substantial improvements in link prediction accuracy, with an average gain of 12.3% over state-of-the-art baselines. This work provides a principled foundation for knowledge engineering in graph mining, opening new avenues for semantic-aware neural network architectures.

Detecting concept drift in high-velocity data streams remains a critical challenge for adaptive machine learning systems. Existing drift detection methods rely on statistical thresholds that fail to adapt to varying data characteristics, leading to either excessive false alarms or delayed detection. This paper presents a theoretically grounded approach to adaptive drift detection based on non-parametric change point analysis. We derive novel concentration inequalities for monitoring distributional shifts in multi-dimensional data streams, enabling theoretically guaranteed detection bounds with adaptive sensitivity. The proposed method introduces a dynamic threshold mechanism that automatically adjusts to local data variance, eliminating the need for manual parameter tuning. Rigorous theoretical analysis establishes that our approach achieves optimal detection delay under the minimax criterion while maintaining bounded false positive rates. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world streaming datasets demonstrate that the proposed method reduces detection latency by 34% compared to state-of-the-art approaches while preserving false alarm rates. This work significantly advances the theoretical foundations of data stream analysis and provides practical tools for real-time knowledge discovery systems.

Modern data integration platforms face unprecedented challenges in maintaining quality across heterogeneous, distributed data sources. This paper presents KQI, a comprehensive knowledge quality intelligence system that fundamentally reimagines data quality management through end-to-end provenance tracking and automated repair. The system introduces a novel knowledge graph representation that captures data lineage, quality metrics, and inter-dependency relationships in a unified framework, enabling holistic quality assessment beyond traditional constraint-based approaches. KQI employs a distributed architecture with three core components: semantic enrichment engine, quality inference engine, and autonomous repair engine. The semantic enrichment engine utilizes pre-trained language models to infer implicit quality constraints from data patterns, while the quality inference engine applies probabilistic reasoning over the knowledge graph to identify systemic quality issues. The autonomous repair engine generates optimal repair strategies that minimize information loss while maximizing quality improvement. We deploy KQI in production environments processing over 10 billion records daily, demonstrating linear scalability and sub-second latency for quality assessment queries. Experiments across three enterprise data warehouses show that KQI improves data quality scores by 47% on average while reducing manual quality management effort by 89%.

Social network analysis at scale demands efficient processing of dynamic graphs with billions of edges and complex interaction patterns. Existing distributed graph processing systems suffer from either excessive communication overhead or limited expressiveness in modeling temporal dependencies. This paper presents StreamGraph, a distributed system for real-time social network analysis that significantly improves throughput and latency through novel optimization techniques. StreamGraph introduces a hybrid partition strategy that balances graph structure locality with temporal coherence, reducing cross-partition communication by 61% compared to hash-based partitioning. The system implements a streaming computation model that unifies batch and incremental processing, enabling complex analytical queries such as temporal community detection and influence propagation with sub-second latency. We design an efficient memory management scheme with adaptive checkpointing that ensures fault tolerance while minimizing overhead. The system achieves a throughput of 2.3 million edge updates per second on a 128-node cluster, representing a 3.2x improvement over state-of-the-art distributed graph engines. StreamGraph has been deployed for analyzing a major social media platform with 500 million active users, demonstrating production-ready performance and reliability.
